```{r}
library(robotcompR)
```

## Forward kinematics

For a tree, the pose of every link follows from a single pass from the base
outward. `robot_fk()` returns the end-effector pose by default, any named
frame, or all frames.

```{r}
arm <- robot_example("planar2")
q <- c(0.6, -1.1)
robot_fk(arm, q)
# Closed form for unit links.
c(cos(q[1]) + cos(q[1] + q[2]), sin(q[1]) + sin(q[1] + q[2]))
```

Batches of configurations go one per row:

```{r}
Q <- rbind(c(0, 0), c(pi / 2, 0), c(pi / 2, pi / 2))
robot_fk_positions(arm, Q)
```

```{r, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 5}
robot_plot_workspace(arm, n = 1500, seed = 1)
```

## The geometric Jacobian

The geometric Jacobian $J(q)$ maps joint velocities to the spatial velocity
of a point on the end effector, linear part first:

$$
\begin{pmatrix} v \\ \omega \end{pmatrix} = J(q) \, \dot q.
$$

For a revolute joint $i$ with world axis $z_i$ through point $p_i$, column $i$
is $(z_i \times (p - p_i), \; z_i)$; for a prismatic joint it is $(z_i, 0)$.

`reference = "world"` expresses both parts in world coordinates at the
end-effector origin. `"local"` expresses them in the end-effector frame, and
`"space"` returns the spatial (twist) Jacobian at the world origin.

```{r}
J <- robot_jacobian(arm, q)
round(J, 6)
Jn <- robot_jacobian_numeric(arm, q)
max(abs(J - Jn))
```

The analytic Jacobian differentiates a minimal orientation parametrization
instead. It becomes singular where that parametrization does, which is why
the geometric Jacobian is preferred for control.

```{r}
puma <- robot_example("puma560")
qp <- c(0.1, -0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0.4, -0.3)
round(robot_jacobian_analytic(puma, qp, representation = "rpy"), 4)
```

## Manipulability and singularities

Yoshikawa's measure $w = \sqrt{\det(J J^\top)}$ is zero at singularities.
robotcompR reports the product of the singular values of the selected rows,
which equals $w$ when there are no more rows than joints. A planar arm has
an identically zero $z$ row, so select `rows = 1:2` for the classical value.
The condition number of the translational block measures isotropy.

```{r}
m <- robot_manipulability(arm, q, rows = 1:2)
m$yoshikawa
abs(sin(q[2]))  # closed form for unit links
m$condition
robot_manipulability(arm, c(0.3, 0), rows = 1:2)$condition
robot_is_singular(arm, c(0.3, 0))
```

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
elbow <- seq(-pi, pi, length.out = 181)
w <- sapply(elbow, function(t) robot_manipulability(arm, c(0, t), rows = 1:2)$yoshikawa)
plot(elbow, w, type = "l", xlab = "elbow angle (rad)", ylab = "manipulability")
```

## Inverse kinematics

`robot_ik()` solves $\min_q e(q)^\top W e(q) = \|W^{1/2} e(q)\|^2$, where $e$
stacks the position error and the rotation-vector orientation error and
$W = \operatorname{diag}(\text{weights})$. Three methods are available:

* `"levenberg_marquardt"` (default): damping scaled by the largest diagonal
  entry of $J^\top W J$, adapted after each accepted or rejected step.
* `"damped_least_squares"`: fixed damping $\lambda$, robust near
  singularities.
* `"pseudoinverse"`: Gauss-Newton with backtracking.

Steps are limited to `max_step` radians or meters. Joint limits are enforced
by projection, and joints pushed against a limit are frozen for that step
(an active set) so the others keep moving. When a run does not converge,
up to `restarts` (default 5) further runs start from random configurations
drawn with a fixed `seed`, so results are reproducible and the global
random state is untouched.

```{r}
target <- robot_fk(puma, qp)
sol <- robot_ik(puma, target, initial = rep(0, 6))
sol$converged
c(position = sol$position_error, orientation = sol$orientation_error)
sol$iterations
max(abs(robot_fk(puma, sol$q)$matrix - target$matrix))
```

Inverse kinematics is rarely unique. The returned solution depends on the
initial guess:

```{r}
s1 <- robot_ik(arm, robot_pose(translation = c(1, 1, 0)), initial = c(0, 1),
               weights = c(1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0))
s2 <- robot_ik(arm, robot_pose(translation = c(1, 1, 0)), initial = c(1.5, -1),
               weights = c(1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0))
rbind(s1$q, s2$q)
ik_planar2(1, 1, 1, 1)
```

Unreachable targets are reported, not hidden. The solver returns the closest
configuration it found, `converged = FALSE`, and a reach bound:

```{r}
far <- robot_ik(arm, robot_pose(translation = c(3, 0, 0)),
                weights = c(1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0))
far$converged
far$position_error
far$reach_bound
far$target_distance
```

Weights select which components matter. A planar arm cannot control all six,
so here only $x$ and $y$ are weighted. For a 6 DOF arm, a zero weight on the
yaw row would ask only for position and two tilt angles.

## Limits

```{r}
lim <- robot_ik(puma, target, initial = rep(0, 6), respect_limits = TRUE)
robot_within_limits(puma, lim$q)
lim$active_limits
```
